claim: Translational efficiency correlates with longevity.
source: Translational efficiency correlates with longevity, yet its role in lifespan determination remains unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established relationship, though the manuscript notes the mechanism remains unclear.

claim: Translation efficiency is globally reduced during replicative aging in budding yeast.
source: Using ribosome profiling, translation efficiency is globally reduced during replicative aging in budding yeast by at least two mechanisms
evidence: This claim is supported by ribosome profiling data presented in the manuscript (Figure 2).

claim: Ssd1 is induced during aging.
source: Firstly, Ssd1 is induced during aging, sequestering mRNAs to P-bodies.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased Ssd1 protein levels in old cells (Figure 1B).

claim: Ssd1 sequesters mRNAs to P-bodies during aging.
source: Firstly, Ssd1 is induced during aging, sequestering mRNAs to P-bodies.
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data showing increased P-body aggregation in old cells (Figure 1C, D) and the known function of Ssd1.

claim: Ssd1 overexpression in young cells reduced translation and extended lifespan.
source: Furthermore, Ssd1 overexpression in young cells reduced translation and extended lifespan
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data (Figure 1E) and replicative lifespan analysis (Figure 1G).

claim: Loss of Ssd1 reduced the translational deficit of old cells and shortened lifespan.
source: while loss of Ssd1 reduced the translational deficit of old cells and shortened lifespan.
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data (Figure 4G) and replicative lifespan analysis (Figure 1F).

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α, mediated by the stress kinase Gcn2, was elevated in old cells.
source: Secondly, phosphorylation of eIF2α, mediated by the stress kinase Gcn2, was elevated in old cells, contributing to the global reduction in translation without detectable induction of the downstream Gcn4 transcriptional activator.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing increased eIF2α phosphorylation in old cells (Figure 4A, B).

claim: Elevated eIF2α phosphorylation in old cells contributes to the global reduction in translation without detectable induction of Gcn4.
source: Secondly, phosphorylation of eIF2α, mediated by the stress kinase Gcn2, was elevated in old cells, contributing to the global reduction in translation without detectable induction of the downstream Gcn4 transcriptional activator.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data (Figure 4A, B), Gcn4-luciferase reporter data (Figure 4E), and ribosome profiling data (Figure 4F).

claim: tRNA overexpression activated Gcn2 in young cells and extended lifespan in a manner dependent on Gcn4.
source: tRNA overexpression activated Gcn2 in young cells and extended lifespan in a manner dependent on Gcn4.
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data showing eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 5C), replicative lifespan analysis (Figure 5B, F, G), and genetic deletion experiments.

claim: Overexpression of Gcn4 sufficed to extend lifespan in an autophagy-dependent manner in the absence of changes in global translation.
source: Moreover, overexpression of Gcn4 sufficed to extend lifespan in an autophagy-dependent manner in the absence of changes in global translation, indicating that Gcn4-mediated autophagy induction is the ultimate downstream target of activated Gcn2, to extend lifespan.
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis (Figure 6A, E, F), polysome profiling (Figure 6C), and autophagy assays (Figure 6D).

claim: Gcn4-mediated autophagy induction is the ultimate downstream target of activated Gcn2 to extend lifespan.
source: Moreover, overexpression of Gcn4 sufficed to extend lifespan in an autophagy-dependent manner in the absence of changes in global translation, indicating that Gcn4-mediated autophagy induction is the ultimate downstream target of activated Gcn2, to extend lifespan.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of Gcn4 overexpression extending lifespan in an autophagy-dependent manner and tRNA overexpression extending lifespan in a Gcn4-dependent manner.

claim: Budding yeast has become a leading model system for aging studies due to its short lifespan, ease of genetic and environmental manipulations, and conserved aging pathways.
source: While aging studies in mammals are slow due to their long lifespans, the single-celled eukaryote budding yeast has become a leading model system for aging studies due to its short lifespan, ease of genetic and environmental manipulations, and conserved aging pathways (Bitterman et al., 2003; Steinkraus et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature establishing yeast as a model system for aging.

claim: Budding yeast represent the only system in which the number of times a cell divides (replicative lifespan) can be accurately determined.
source: Furthermore, budding yeast represent the only system in which the number of times a cell divides, also known as replicative lifespan, can be accurately determined.
evidence: This is stated as an established fact about the unique capabilities of the yeast system.

claim: The mother enrichment program (MEP) enables identification and characterization of molecular changes that accompany replicative aging.
source: Together with recently developed methodologies to isolate larger quantities of old yeast cells, such as the mother enrichment program (MEP) (Lindstrom and Gottschling, 2009), identification and characterization of the molecular changes that accompany, and potentially cause, replicative aging is now feasible, enabling many questions about aging to be answered.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the MEP methodology and its application in this study.

claim: When nutrients are abundant and cells are growing, the target of rapamycin (TOR) kinase is active.
source: When nutrients are abundant and cells are growing, the target of rapamycin (TOR) kinase is active, phosphorylating and inactivating the 4EBP1 repressor of CAP-dependent translation and activating the S6 kinase 1 to promote ribosome biogenesis via phosphorylation of Rps6 (Blenis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about TOR signaling.

claim: Active TOR phosphorylates and inactivates the 4EBP1 repressor of CAP-dependent translation.
source: When nutrients are abundant and cells are growing, the target of rapamycin (TOR) kinase is active, phosphorylating and inactivating the 4EBP1 repressor of CAP-dependent translation and activating the S6 kinase 1 to promote ribosome biogenesis via phosphorylation of Rps6 (Blenis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about TOR signaling.

claim: Active TOR activates S6 kinase 1 to promote ribosome biogenesis via phosphorylation of Rps6.
source: When nutrients are abundant and cells are growing, the target of rapamycin (TOR) kinase is active, phosphorylating and inactivating the 4EBP1 repressor of CAP-dependent translation and activating the S6 kinase 1 to promote ribosome biogenesis via phosphorylation of Rps6 (Blenis, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about TOR signaling.

claim: In response to limited growth or limited nutrients, global CAP-dependent translation is repressed due to TOR inactivation.
source: In response to limited growth or limited nutrients, global CAP-dependent translation is repressed due to TOR inactivation and the accompanying dephosphorylation of 4EBP1 and Sch9 in mammalian cells, while in yeast TOR inactivation reduces global translation via reduced gene expression of ribosomal protein genes (Martin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about TOR signaling.

claim: In yeast, TOR inactivation reduces global translation via reduced gene expression of ribosomal protein genes.
source: In response to limited growth or limited nutrients, global CAP-dependent translation is repressed due to TOR inactivation and the accompanying dephosphorylation of 4EBP1 and Sch9 in mammalian cells, while in yeast TOR inactivation reduces global translation via reduced gene expression of ribosomal protein genes (Martin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on yeast TOR signaling.

claim: Stress-induced activation of stress response kinases results in inhibitory phosphorylation of eIF2α.
source: A distinct parallel pathway that reduces global protein synthesis is stress-induced activation of the stress response kinase(s) that result in inhibitory phosphorylation of eIF2α (Donnelly et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about stress response pathways.

claim: In yeast, the only eIF2α kinase is Gcn2.
source: There are multiple stress response kinases that phosphorylate eIF2α in mammals in response to different stresses, but in yeast the only eIF2α kinase is Gcn2.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about yeast stress response pathways.

claim: Yeast Gcn2 is activated by salt stress, acid, oxidative stress and by uncharged tRNAs that accumulate when intracellular amino acid levels are low.
source: Yeast Gcn2 is activated by salt stress, acid, oxidative stress and by the uncharged tRNAs that accumulate when intracellular amino acid levels are low (Gallinetti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Gcn2 activation.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α results in globally reduced efficiency of translational initiation.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α results in globally reduced efficiency of translational initiation while paradoxically inducing translation of the Gcn4 transcriptional regulator (the yeast counterpart of ATF4) due to leaky scanning of ribosomes through its inhibitory upstream open reading frames (uORFs) to the GCN4 ORF (Gallinetti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about eIF2α phosphorylation.

claim: Phosphorylation of eIF2α paradoxically induces translation of the Gcn4 transcriptional regulator due to leaky scanning of ribosomes through its inhibitory upstream open reading frames (uORFs) to the GCN4 ORF.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α results in globally reduced efficiency of translational initiation while paradoxically inducing translation of the Gcn4 transcriptional regulator (the yeast counterpart of ATF4) due to leaky scanning of ribosomes through its inhibitory upstream open reading frames (uORFs) to the GCN4 ORF (Gallinetti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to established knowledge about Gcn4 translation regulation.

claim: Gcn4 is the yeast counterpart of ATF4.
source: Phosphorylation of eIF2α results in globally reduced efficiency of translational initiation while paradoxically inducing translation of the Gcn4 transcriptional regulator (the yeast counterpart of ATF4) due to leaky scanning of ribosomes through its inhibitory upstream open reading frames (uORFs) to the GCN4 ORF (Gallinetti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the relationship between yeast and mammalian stress response factors.

claim: Gcn4 induces expression of genes that mediate amino acid biosynthesis, purine biosynthesis, organelle biosynthesis, ER stress response, mitochondrial carrier proteins and autophagy.
source: Gcn4 induces expression of a variety of genes that mediate amino acid biosynthesis, purine biosynthesis, organelle biosynthesis, ER stress response, mitochondrial carrier proteins and autophagy (Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016), while also repressing genes encoding the translation machinery and ribosomes (Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Gcn4 function.

claim: Gcn4 represses genes encoding the translation machinery and ribosomes.
source: Gcn4 induces expression of a variety of genes that mediate amino acid biosynthesis, purine biosynthesis, organelle biosynthesis, ER stress response, mitochondrial carrier proteins and autophagy (Pakos-Zebrucka et al., 2016), while also repressing genes encoding the translation machinery and ribosomes (Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Gcn4 function.

claim: Manipulations that mildly lower the rate of protein synthesis often also lower the rate of aging, increasing the lifespan of organisms from yeast to humans.
source: Manipulations that mildly lower the rate of protein synthesis often also lower the rate of aging, increasing the lifespan of organisms from yeast to humans (Tavernarakis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of the literature on protein synthesis and aging.

claim: The TOR pathway is a conserved player in longevity.
source: For example, the TOR pathway is a conserved player in longevity, where it regulates many processes such as transcription, autophagy, cytoskeletal organization, protein turnover and mRNA translation (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on TOR and longevity.

claim: Inactivation of TOR reduces protein synthesis and extends lifespan in organisms from yeast to mice.
source: Inactivation of TOR, for example by the drug rapamycin, reduces protein synthesis and extends lifespan in organisms from yeast to mice (Blagosklonny, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on TOR inhibition and lifespan.

claim: Loss of one specific isoform of eIF4E in C. elegans extends lifespan.
source: In particular, eIF4E facilitates the recruitment of ribosomes to the mRNA, which is a major rate-limiting step in protein synthesis. Loss of one specific isoform of eIF4E in C. elegans extends lifespan (Syntichaki et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on eIF4E and lifespan in C. elegans.

claim: Reducing the levels of certain eIFs or large ribosomal subunits reduces protein synthesis and extends organismal lifespan in worms, flies and yeast.
source: Similarly, reducing the levels of other eIFs, or certain large ribosomal subunits, reduces protein synthesis and extends organismal lifespan in worms, flies and yeast (Hansen et al., 2007; Pan et al., 2007; Chen et al., 2007; Curran and Ruvkun, 2007; Steffen et al., 2008; McCormick et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies on translation factors and lifespan.

claim: The protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide extends lifespan in C. elegans and delays senescence in normal human fibroblasts.
source: The protein synthesis inhibitor cycloheximide also extends lifespan in C. elegans and delays senescence in normal human fibroblasts (Takauji et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on cycloheximide and aging.

claim: Not all manipulations that reduce global protein synthesis extend lifespan, such as depletion of most yeast small ribosomal subunits.
source: However, not all manipulations that reduce global protein synthesis extend lifespan, such as depletion of most yeast small ribosomal subunits (Steffen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research showing exceptions to the protein synthesis-lifespan relationship.

claim: The full yeast lifespan extension that results from depletion of large ribosomal subunits, TOR1 deletion, or dietary restriction, requires the transcriptional regulator Gcn4.
source: Notably, the full yeast lifespan extension that results from depletion of large ribosomal subunits, TOR1 deletion, or dietary restriction, requires the transcriptional regulator Gcn4 (Steffen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Gcn4 and lifespan extension.

claim: During the normal aging process, global protein synthesis generally declines with increased organismal age.
source: During the normal aging process, where examined, global protein synthesis generally declines with increased organismal age (Tavernarakis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of the literature on protein synthesis and aging.

claim: Elevated levels of protein synthesis have been observed during premature aging, as seen in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome.
source: Conversely, elevated levels of protein synthesis have been observed during premature aging, as seen in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (Buchwalter and Hetzer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on protein synthesis in progeria.

claim: Histone protein levels go down during replicative aging despite increased histone transcript levels and no change in the half-life of histone proteins.
source: We previously suggested that histone protein synthesis may be reduced during yeast replicative aging (Feser et al., 2010). This was based on the observation that levels of histone proteins go down during replicative aging, causing aging, despite increased histone transcript levels and no change in the half-life of histone proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work on histone levels during aging.

claim: The abundance of virtually every transcript encoded by the yeast genome increases during replicative aging, with the exception of those that are highly abundant already.
source: We have shown previously that the abundance of virtually every transcript encoded by the yeast genome increases during replicative aging, with the exception of those that are highly abundant already, such as those encoding the ribosome protein genes, which do not significantly change during aging (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work on transcript abundance during aging.

claim: Old yeast cells isolated by the MEP had undergone an average of 25-30 divisions, where the median replicative lifespan is 22 divisions.
source: In these analyses, we isolated budding yeast cells that had undergone an average of 25–30 divisions, where the median replicative lifespan is 22 divisions, using the MEP as described previously (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated as a description of the experimental methods used in this study.

claim: Young cells had mRNAs bound to 1-5 ribosomes, while old cells showed extremely low levels of RNA on polysomes.
source: While young cells had mRNAs bound to 1–5 ribosomes, old cells showed extremely low levels of RNA on polysomes (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: In old cells, RNA was not only less polysome-associated but also less monosome-associated, providing evidence that translational initiation is extremely low.
source: In old cells, the RNA was not only less polysome-associated but also less monosome-associated, providing evidence that translational initiation is extremely low (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 1A and interpreted by the authors.

claim: The reduced protein synthesis in old cells is not a consequence of accumulation of dead cells, because the old cells isolated by the mother enrichment program are still viable.
source: This is not a consequence of accumulation of dead cells, because the old cells isolated by the mother enrichment program are still viable (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work demonstrating viability of old cells isolated by MEP.

claim: rRNA levels are equivalent during aging.
source: Notably, rRNA levels are equivalent during aging (Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on rRNA levels during aging.

claim: There is a striking defect in global protein synthesis in replicatively aged yeast.
source: These results indicate that there is a striking defect in global protein synthesis in replicatively aged yeast.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the polysome profiling data presented in Figure 1A.

claim: SSD1 was upregulated during aging but not upon experimental depletion of histone H3.
source: In an effort to uncover genes that influence longevity, we identified a small subset of genes that were upregulated during aging (which was mostly due to histone loss during aging), but not upon experimental depletion of histone H3 (Hu et al., 2014). One of these genes, SSD1, was of particular interest with regard to reduced protein synthesis during aging, because it is an mRNA binding protein that can function as a translational repressor (Jansen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work on gene expression during aging.

claim: SSD1 is an mRNA binding protein that can function as a translational repressor.
source: One of these genes, SSD1, was of particular interest with regard to reduced protein synthesis during aging, because it is an mRNA binding protein that can function as a translational repressor (Jansen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 function.

claim: A C-terminal truncation mutation within the SSD1 gene is responsible for the short lifespan of certain yeast strain backgrounds.
source: Furthermore, a C-terminal truncation mutation within the SSD1 gene had been shown to be responsible for the short lifespan of certain yeast strain backgrounds, while long-lived yeast strain backgrounds have wild type SSD1 (Kaeberlein et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 and lifespan.

claim: Long-lived yeast strain backgrounds have wild type SSD1.
source: Furthermore, a C-terminal truncation mutation within the SSD1 gene had been shown to be responsible for the short lifespan of certain yeast strain backgrounds, while long-lived yeast strain backgrounds have wild type SSD1 (Kaeberlein et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 and lifespan.

claim: Ssd1 protein levels were greatly increased in old cells.
source: Therefore, we confirmed that Ssd1 protein levels were in fact greatly increased in old cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ssd1 normally delivers mRNAs to daughter cells for translation.
source: Ssd1 normally delivers mRNAs to daughter cells for translation but in response to stress, Ssd1 transports mRNAs to cytoplasmic aggregates of P-bodies (Kurischko et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 function.

claim: In response to stress, Ssd1 transports mRNAs to cytoplasmic aggregates of P-bodies.
source: Ssd1 normally delivers mRNAs to daughter cells for translation but in response to stress, Ssd1 transports mRNAs to cytoplasmic aggregates of P-bodies (Kurischko et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 function.

claim: Aggregated P-bodies became much more abundant in old yeast, where more than 85% of old cells showed visible P-bodies compared to only 1% in young cells.
source: Aggregated P-bodies, visualized as cytoplasmic puncta containing the P-body protein Lsm1 (Lsm1-GFP) and Pab1-GFP (data not shown), became much more abundant in old yeast (Figure 1C), where more than 85% of old cells showed visible P-bodies compared to only 1% in young cells (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 1C and quantitation in Figure 1D.

claim: Ssd1-GFP co-localized with P-bodies in old cells.
source: In addition, Ssd1-GFP co-localized with P-bodies in old cells (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from fluorescence microscopy, though the data is not shown.

claim: Aggregated P-bodies accumulate during replicative aging.
source: These results show that aggregated P-bodies accumulate during replicative aging and it is likely that the age-induced Ssd1 targets mRNA to the P-bodies leading to down-regulation of their protein synthesis in old cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microscopy data showing increased P-bodies in old cells.

claim: The age-induced Ssd1 likely targets mRNA to the P-bodies leading to down-regulation of their protein synthesis in old cells.
source: These results show that aggregated P-bodies accumulate during replicative aging and it is likely that the age-induced Ssd1 targets mRNA to the P-bodies leading to down-regulation of their protein synthesis in old cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of increased Ssd1, increased P-bodies, and reduced protein synthesis in old cells.

claim: High-level overexpression of Ssd1 is lethal.
source: High-level overexpression of Ssd1 is known to be lethal (Sopko et al., 2006), so we moderately overexpressed Ssd1 using 0.5% galactose to induce SSD1 under the galactose-inducible GAL1 promoter.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 overexpression.

claim: Cell growth is slower in galactose.
source: Cell growth is slower in galactose, accounting for the reduced protein synthesis in the wild type cells apparent in the polysome profile (Figure 1E) as compared to yeast grown in glucose (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about yeast growth in different carbon sources.

claim: Moderate overexpression of Ssd1 reduced protein synthesis compared to wild type cells.
source: Despite this, it is clear that moderate overexpression of Ssd1 reduced protein synthesis compared to that in wild type cells (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: In a growing culture of yeast, most cells are predominantly young.
source: In a growing culture of yeast, 50% of the cells have divided 0 times, 25% have divided once, 12.5% have divided twice etc., such that most cells in a yeast culture are predominantly young.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of exponential growth in yeast cultures.

claim: Elevated Ssd1 levels are sufficient to reduce protein synthesis in young cells.
source: As such, these data indicate that elevated Ssd1 levels are sufficient to reduce protein synthesis in young cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the polysome profiling data of Ssd1 overexpression in young cells.

claim: The absence of Ssd1 significantly shortened replicative lifespan.
source: The absence of Ssd1, achieved by glucose–mediated repression of pGAL1-SSD1, significantly shortened replicative lifespan (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Moderate overexpression of Ssd1 significantly extended lifespan.
source: Conversely, moderate overexpression of Ssd1 significantly extended lifespan (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Ssd1 function is required for yeast to achieve a normal lifespan.
source: These results indicate that Ssd1 function, presumably in translational repression, is required for yeast to achieve a normal lifespan, while overexpression of Ssd1 can extend yeast lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lifespan data showing shortened lifespan upon Ssd1 loss.

claim: The age-induced increase in Ssd1 levels may be at least partially responsible for the age-related decline of global protein synthesis.
source: Taken together with the reduced protein synthesis that occurs upon Ssd1 overexpression in young cells (Figure 1E), these data suggest that the age-induced increase in Ssd1 levels may be at least partially responsible for the age-related decline of global protein synthesis.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of Ssd1 induction in old cells, reduced protein synthesis upon Ssd1 overexpression, and restoration of protein synthesis upon Ssd1 deletion in old cells.

claim: Translation in general decreases during aging, as seen by Ribo-seq analysis.
source: Ribo-seq analysis, performed three times from independent samples for young, middle aged and old yeast, showed that translation in general decreases during aging, as seen by the increased amount of blue and reduction of yellow in the Ribo-seq heat map, as the cells became older (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The abundance of most transcripts increase during aging.
source: This confirmed that the abundance of m transcripts increase during aging (Figure 2B) (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2B and citation to previous work.

claim: There is an increase in cryptic transcription within genes during aging.
source: We also observed an increase in cryptic (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) transcription within genes during aging, as seen previously (Sen et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and citation to previous work.

claim: There is increased intergenic transcription during aging consistent with reduced histone occupancy during aging.
source: and intergenic (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) transcription during aging consistent with the reduced histone occupancy during aging (Hu et al., 2014) promoting access by the general transcription machinery to cryptic initiation sites.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and citation to previous work on histone occupancy.

claim: Translational efficiency decreased globally during aging, with 59% of genes (3472 out of 6553) showing up to 40-fold reduction.
source: Translational efficiency significantly decreased up to 40 fold during aging for 59% of the genes in the yeast genome (3472 out of 6553), while the remainder of the transcripts had no significant change in translational efficiency during aging (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by translational efficiency analysis shown in Figure 2C and 2D.

claim: The reduction in translational efficiency was already apparent in middle-aged yeast (median age of 12 divisions).
source: The reduction in translational efficiency was already apparent in middle-aged yeast (median age of 12 divisions), albeit becoming more pronounced in the old yeast (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by translational efficiency analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: There is no evidence for increased translational pausing or elongation defects during aging.
source: We found no evidence for increased translational pausing or elongation defects during aging which are characterized by increased peaks of ribosomes within ORFs and general enrichment of ribosomes within the ORF relative to the start of the ORF (Ingolia, 2016), respectively (Figure 2—figure supplement 5)
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The rate-limiting step in protein synthesis during aging is initiation.
source: suggesting that the rate-limiting step in protein synthesis during aging is initiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of evidence for elongation defects and the observed reduction in monosome-associated RNA.

claim: Translation efficiency went down the most during aging for the transcripts that were the most abundant in young cells.
source: Upon comparing the transcript abundance for every gene in young cells to the change in translational efficiency during aging, it was apparent that translation efficiency went down the most during aging for the transcripts that were the most abundant in young cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The greatest reduction in translational efficiency during aging was seen for genes encoding ribosomal proteins or other proteins required for protein synthesis or its regulation.
source: The greatest reduction in translational efficiency during aging was seen for genes encoding ribosomal proteins, or other proteins required for protein synthesis or its regulation (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis and specific examples shown in Figures 3B-D and supplements.

claim: Transcripts that were least abundant in young cells did not have a significant change in translation efficiency during aging.
source: Transcripts that were least abundant in young cells did not have a significant change in translation efficiency (Figure 3A) and functioned in a broad variety of pathways (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 3A and gene ontology analysis in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Phosphorylation of the Gcn2 target eIF2α is clearly apparent in old but not young cells.
source: We found that phosphorylation of the Gcn2 target eIF2α is clearly apparent in old but not young cells (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The level of eIF2α phosphorylation in old cells was almost as much as that achieved by depletion of amino acids to 20% of their normal levels.
source: The level of eIF2α phosphorylation in old cells was almost as much as that achieved by depletion of amino acids to 20% of their normal levels, which is a known condition that activates Gcn2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B comparing old cells to amino acid depleted cells.

claim: Striking TOR inhibition was not apparent in old cells, because the S6K1-mediated phosphorylation of Rps6 persisted.
source: By contrast, striking TOR inhibition was not apparent in old cells, because the S6K1-mediated phosphorylation of Rps6 persisted (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4B showing persistent Rps6 phosphorylation in old cells.

claim: Old cells are experiencing a stress condition that is sensed specifically by Gcn2.
source: These data are consistent with old cells experiencing a stress condition that is sensed specifically by Gcn2.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of eIF2α phosphorylation without TOR inhibition in old cells.

claim: There is a positive correlation (r = 0.614) between genes with the greatest reduction in translational efficiency during replicative aging and those with the greatest reduction during amino acid starvation.
source: Accordingly, we observed a positive correlation (r = 0.614) between the two data sets, where the genes with the greatest reduction in translational efficiency during replicative aging tended to have the greatest reduction in translational efficiency during Gcn2 activation by amino acid starvation (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the authors' data with published data from Ingolia et al., 2009, shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 122 transcripts have increased translation during amino acid depletion but not during aging.
source: We found that 122 transcripts have increased translation during amino acid depletion but not during aging (Figure 4C), and these tend to encode proteins involved in the stress response pathways that are induced by amino acid starvation (Ingolia et al., 2009) (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of the authors' data with published data, shown in Figure 4C and 4D.

claim: Genes with increased translation during amino acid depletion but not during aging were significantly enriched in genes upregulated during Gcn4 overexpression and with Gcn4 consensus sites in their promoters.
source: The genes that had increased translation during amino acid depletion but not during aging were significantly enriched in the 40 genes that are upregulated during Gcn4 overexpression and with the approximately 60 genes with Gcn4 consensus sites in their promoters (Figure 4—figure supplement 3) (Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and citation to previous work on Gcn4 targets.

claim: There is no significant upregulation of a Gcn4-luciferase reporter in old cells.
source: In agreement with failure to observe translation of the transcripts activated by Gcn4 during aging, we find that even though levels of phosphorylated eIF2α are higher during aging (Figure 4A,B), we do not find significant upregulation of a Gcn4-luciferase reporter in old cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by Gcn4-luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Translation of the endogenous Gcn4 was not increased in old cells.
source: Furthermore, translation of the endogenous Gcn4 was not increased in old cells, apparent in the ribosome profile over the Gcn4 transcript (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data over the GCN4 locus shown in Figure 4F.

claim: There was less translation of the GCN4 upstream ORFs in old cells, but this was not sufficient to lead to increased translation of the Gcn4 ORF.
source: While there was less translation of the GCN4 upstream ORFs in old cells, this was not sufficient to lead to increased translation of the Gcn4 ORF (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by ribosome profiling data over the GCN4 locus shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Gcn4 and its downstream targets are not upregulated in old cells.
source: Consistent with this, we did not observe preferential transcriptional activation or repression of Gcn4 targets during aging (Hu et al., 2014). In summary, consistent with the elevated levels of phosphorylation of eIF2α in old cells, the global reduction of translational initiation in old cells is similar to that seen during stress conditions that induce eIF2α phosphorylation (Kimball, 1999), with the major difference being that Gcn4 and its downstream targets are not upregulated in old cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to the authors' previous work and comparison with published data on stress responses.

claim: Deletion of either GCN2 or SSD1 restored the monosome peak that is absent in old wild type yeast.
source: By specifically examining polysome profiles from old yeast, it was apparent that deletion of either gene GCN2 or SSD1 restored the monosome peak that is absent in the old wild type yeast (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 4G (note: text says 4F but likely refers to 4G).

claim: Deletion of both GCN2 and SSD1 further restored protein synthesis in old cells.
source: Furthermore, deletion of both GCN2 and SSD1 further restored the protein synthesis in old cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 4G (note: text says 4F but likely refers to 4G).

claim: Ssd1 induction and Gcn2 activity each contribute to the down-regulation of protein synthesis that occurs during replicative aging.
source: These results indicate that Ssd1 induction and Gcn2 activity each contribute to the down-regulation of protein synthesis that occurs during replicative aging.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the polysome profiling data of deletion mutants in old cells.

claim: Overexpression of IMT4 (encoding an initiator tRNAMET) creates uncharged tRNAs and led to a significant increase in replicative lifespan.
source: Given that Gcn2 can be activated by uncharged tRNAs (i.e. tRNAs not bound to amino acids), we overexpressed IMT4, which encodes an initiator tRNAMET. Overexperssion of IMT4 from a 2μ vector creates uncharged tRNAs, and this led to a significant increase in replicative lifespan compared to isogenic cells carrying the empty 2μ vector using both a survival assay time course that measures the ability of the aging mothers to form colonies over a time course of the MEP (Figure 5A) and the micromanipulation assay (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: tRNA overexpression resulted in Gcn2 activation in young cells, reflected by eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: tRNA overexpression resulted in Gcn2 activation in young cells, reflected by eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 5C), but had no influence on Rps6 phosphorylation suggesting that it did not inactivate TOR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C (note: text says 5B for Rps6 but likely refers to 5C).

claim: tRNA overexpression had no influence on Rps6 phosphorylation suggesting that it did not inactivate TOR.
source: tRNA overexpression resulted in Gcn2 activation in young cells, reflected by eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 5C), but had no influence on Rps6 phosphorylation suggesting that it did not inactivate TOR (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C (note: text says 5B but likely refers to 5C).

claim: Gcn2 activation does not inhibit the TOR pathway in yeast, at least in rich media conditions.
source: This result shows that Gcn2 activation does not inhibit the TOR pathway in yeast, at least in rich media conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that tRNA overexpression activates Gcn2 without affecting Rps6 phosphorylation.

claim: Activation of Gcn2 results from TOR inhibition.
source: This is in contrast to the activation of Gcn2 that results from TOR inhibition (Figure 5C) (Cherkasova and Hinnebusch, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 5C and citation to previous work.

claim: tRNA overexpression induced the Gcn4-luciferase reporter to equivalent levels as amino acid starvation, in a manner that was dependent on Gcn2.
source: Furthermore, tRNA overexpression induced the Gcn4-luciferase reporter to equivalent levels as amino acid starvation, in a manner that was dependent on Gcn2 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by Gcn4-luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: tRNA overexpression reduced overall protein synthesis in young cells.
source: By polysome analysis, we found that tRNA overexpression reduced overall protein synthesis in young cells (Figure 5E), consistent with induced eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The replicative lifespan extension achieved by IMT4 overexpression was fully dependent on Gcn2.
source: To determine whether overexpression of the tRNA encoded by IMT4 was indeed extending lifespan through the stress response pathway, we deleted the gene encoding the GCN2 kinase. We found that the replicative lifespan extension that was achieved by IMT4 overexpression was fully dependent on Gcn2 (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: GCN2 deletion alone had no effect on lifespan.
source: Notably, GCN2 deletion alone had no effect on lifespan (Figure 5F), indicating that the reduced protein synthesis in old cells that is mediated by eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 4G) does not optimize the normal lifespan.
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The reduced protein synthesis in old cells that is mediated by eIF2α phosphorylation does not optimize the normal lifespan.
source: Notably, GCN2 deletion alone had no effect on lifespan (Figure 5F), indicating that the reduced protein synthesis in old cells that is mediated by eIF2α phosphorylation (Figure 4G) does not optimize the normal lifespan.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that GCN2 deletion does not affect lifespan despite restoring protein synthesis in old cells.

claim: The replicative lifespan extension achieved by IMT4 overexpression was dependent on GCN4.
source: To differentiate between these possibilities, we deleted GCN4 in the context of IMT4 overexpression. We found that the replicative lifespan extension that was achieved by IMT4 overexpression was dependent on GCN4 (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: tRNA overexpression activates Gcn2 to extend replicative lifespan in a manner seemingly independent of TOR inactivation but dependent on Gcn4.
source: These results show that tRNA overexpression activates Gcn2 to extend replicative lifespan, in a manner seemingly independent of TOR inactivation, but dependent on Gcn4.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combination of lifespan, Western blot, and genetic deletion data.

claim: Overexpression of Gcn4 significantly extended lifespan.
source: In comparison to an isogenic control, overexpression of Gcn4 significantly extended lifespan (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Overexpression of Gcn4 led to no apparent induction of Gcn2 activity or inhibition of TOR activity.
source: Importantly, overexpression of Gcn4 led to no apparent induction of Gcn2 activity or inhibition of TOR activity (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Gcn4 translation is sufficient to extend replicative lifespan in a manner seemingly independent of TOR inhibition.
source: As such, Gcn4 translation is sufficient to extend replicative lifespan in a manner seemingly independent of TOR inhibition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lifespan extension by Gcn4 overexpression without TOR inhibition.

claim: Gcn4 has been reported to repress genes required for protein synthesis.
source: Gcn4 has been reported to repress genes required for protein synthesis (Mittal et al., 2017), but we observed no suppression of global protein synthesis in polysome profiling analysis of young cells overexpressing Gcn4 (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and polysome profiling data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Gcn4 overexpression is sufficient to extend replicative lifespan in the absence of reduced global protein synthesis.
source: These results indicate that Gcn4 overexpression is sufficient to extend replicative lifespan in the absence of reduced global protein synthesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lifespan extension by Gcn4 overexpression without reduced protein synthesis.

claim: Gcn4 overexpression activates autophagy in rich growth conditions.
source: Given the many links between autophagy and aging in other species (Rubinsztein et al., 2011), we asked whether induction of Gcn4 activates autophagy in rich growth conditions. To do this, we used the quantitative Pho8∆60 assay of nonspecific autophagy (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by autophagy assay data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Deletion of ATG1 completely blocked lifespan extension by Gcn4 overexpression.
source: To determine whether the lifespan extension that resulted from Gcn4 overexpression required autophagy we deleted ATG1. While ATG1 deletion alone did not have a significant effect on replicative lifespan compared to wild type, deletion of ATG1 completely blocked lifespan extension by Gcn4 overexpression (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The lifespan extension caused by Gcn4 overexpression requires ATG8.
source: To provide additional evidence for the requirement of autophagy in the lifespan extension mediated by Gcn4 activation, we deleted ATG8 (Figure 6F). The lifespan of the wild type, atg8∆ and atg8∆ GCN4-OX strains were not statistically different, revealing that the lifespan extension caused by Gcn4 overexpression requires ATG8.
evidence: This is supported by replicative lifespan analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Gcn4 induction extends replicative lifespan in a manner that is fully dependent on autophagy.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Gcn4 induction extends replicative lifespan in a manner that is fully dependent on autophagy (Figure 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the autophagy assay and genetic deletion data.

claim: P-body aggregation is mediated by accumulation of stalled preinitiation complexes, especially 40S ribosomes and mRNA.
source: P-body aggregation is known to be mediated by accumulation of stalled preinitiation complexes, especially 40S ribosomes and mRNA (Panas et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on P-body formation.

claim: Inhibition of translation by Gcn2-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation during aging would lead to accumulation of 40S ribosomes and mRNA, which could trigger aggregation of P-bodies in old cells.
source: Inhibition of translation by Gcn2-mediated eIF2α phosphorylation during aging would lead to accumulation of 40S ribosomes and mRNA, which could trigger aggregation of P-bodies in old cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the known mechanism of P-body formation and the observed Gcn2 activation in old cells.

claim: P-bodies accumulate in an age-dependent manner in the somatic cells of adult worms.
source: Our observations are unlikely to be specific to yeast, given that P-bodies accumulate in an age-dependent manner in the somatic cells of adult worms (Rousakis et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on P-bodies in C. elegans aging.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ssd1 by the Cbk1 kinase promotes the role of Ssd1 in delivering mRNAs to the daughter cell for translation.
source: The role of Ssd1 in delivering mRNAs to the daughter cell for translation is promoted by phosphorylation of Ssd1 by the Cbk1 kinase (Jansen et al., 2009; Kurischko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Ssd1 regulation.

claim: The localization of Ssd1 to aggregated P-bodies for translational repression is normally inhibited in non-stressed cells by the phosphorylation of Ssd1 by Cbk1.
source: Meanwhile, the localization of Ssd1 to aggregated P-bodies for translational repression is normally inhibited in non-stressed cells, at least partly by the phosphorylation of Ssd1 by Cbk1 (Jansen et al., 2009; Kurischko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Ssd1 regulation.

claim: Polysome profiles of SSD1 vs. ssd1∆ young cells are indistinguishable, showing no increased translation upon loss of Ssd1.
source: Indeed polysome profiles of SSD1 vs. ssd1∆ young cells are indistinguishable, showing no increased translation upon loss of Ssd1 (Jansen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 function in young cells.

claim: Ssd1 has been reported to bind to 59 and 152 specific mRNAs.
source: It was somewhat surprising that moderate overexpression of Ssd1 globally reduced protein synthesis in young cells (Figure 1E), given that Ssd1 has only been reported to bind to 59 and 152 specific mRNAs (Jansen et al., 2009; Hogan et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Ssd1-bound mRNAs.

claim: Moderate overexpression of Ssd1 causes localization of Ssd1 to aggregated P-bodies under non-stress conditions.
source: In agreement, moderate overexpression of Ssd1 causes localization of Ssd1 to aggregated P-bodies under non-stress conditions, indicating that this overwhelms regulatory Cbk1 phosphorylations (Kurischko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 overexpression.

claim: Glucose depletion causes formation of P-bodies containing Ssd1.
source: Glucose depletion, one of the best known mechanisms to promote longevity, causes formation of P-bodies containing Ssd1 (Kurischko et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Ssd1 localization during stress.

claim: Amino acid depletion led to P-body formation in young yeast.
source: Amino acid depletion, another intervention known to extend yeast replicative lifespan (Lee et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2000) also led to P-body formation in young yeast (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), as it does in mammalian cells (Aizer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by microscopy data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and citations to previous work.

claim: Most Cbk1 localizes asymmetrically to buds.
source: Considering that most Cbk1 localizes asymmetrically to buds (Colman-Lerner et al., 2001), our data are consistent with the model that moderate Ssd1 overexpression overwhelms regulatory Cbk1 phosphorylations in mother cells where Cbk1 concentrations are low, but not in buds where Cbk1 concentrations are higher.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Cbk1 localization.

claim: Ssd1 translation efficiency decreased during aging.
source: Moreover, Ssd1 translation efficiency decreased during aging (Table S1), suggesting that mechanisms may exist to stabilize Ssd1 protein in old cells.
evidence: This is supported by reference to supplementary data (Table S1).

claim: Amino acid depletion is accompanied by increase in levels of Ssd1 protein.
source: Noteworthy, amino acid depletion, a lifespan extending intervention, is also accompanied by increase in levels of Ssd1 protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gcn4 synthesis is induced under many conditions besides amino acid depletion, including starvation for purines, glucose limitation, ER stress, growth on non-fermentable carbon sources, high salt, treatment with alkylating agents, and TOR inhibition.
source: Although Gcn2 is activated by uncharged tRNAs, Gcn4 synthesis, resulting presumably from Gcn2 activation, is induced under many conditions besides amino acid depletion. These include starvation for purines (Rolfes and Hinnebusch, 1993), glucose limitation (Yang et al., 2000), ER stress (Deloche et al., 2004), growth on non-fermentable carbon sources like ethanol (Yang et al., 2000), high salt (Goossens et al., 2001), treatment with alkylating agents (Natarajan et al., 2001) and TOR inhibition (Cherkasova and Hinnebusch, 2003; Kubota et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies on Gcn4 induction.

claim: All conditions that activate Gcn4 depend on the Gcn2 kinase.
source: All these conditions that activate Gcn4 depend on the Gcn2 kinase and many extend yeast replicative lifespan (Postnikoff et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review of the literature on Gcn2 and lifespan.

claim: Deletion of GCN4 reduces the yeast replicative lifespan extension that results from deletion of LOS1 and from deletion of AFG3.
source: Deletion of GCN4 reduces the yeast replicative lifespan extension that results from deletion of LOS1, a tRNA exporter, and from deletion of AFG3, which is involved in mitochondrial mRNA translation (McCormick et al., 2015; Delaney et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on Gcn4 and lifespan extension.

claim: Replicative lifespan can be extended by depletion of the 60S ribosomal subunits in yeast.
source: Replicative lifespan can also be extended by depletion of the 60S ribosomal subunits in yeast (Steffen et al., 2008), which also induces Gcn4 translation (Mittal et al., 2017) and deletion of GCN4 reduces this lifespan extension (Steffen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on ribosomal subunit depletion and lifespan.

claim: Dietary restriction and TOR inhibition increase Gcn4 translation.
source: Dietary restriction and TOR inhibition also increase Gcn4 translation, while GCN4 deletion reduces the ability of TOR inactivation and dietary restriction to extend replicative lifespan (Steffen et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous research on Gcn4 and lifespan extension.

claim: Overexpression of Gcn4 from an ADH1 promoter extends replicative lifespan and reduces bulk protein synthesis.
source: Overexpression of Gcn4 from an ADH1 promoter was very recently shown to extend replicative lifespan and reduce bulk protein synthesis (Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent research on Gcn4 overexpression.

claim: Autophagy is required for lifespan extension in response to mutations that induce ER stress during yeast replicative aging.
source: Although this has mostly been from studies in metazoans or during chronological aging (Rubinsztein et al., 2011; Tyler and Johnson, 2018), a recent study during yeast replicative aging demonstrated that autophagy was required for lifespan extension in response to mutations that induce ER stress (Ghavidel et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research on autophagy and aging.

claim: The TOR pathway and the RAS/PKA pathway inhibit autophagy when nutrients are abundant.
source: The TOR pathway and the RAS/PKA pathway inhibit autophagy when nutrients are abundant.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nutrient sensing pathways.

claim: When nutrients are limiting, the nutrient sensing pathways are inactivated and their inhibitory influence on autophagy is released.
source: However, when nutrients are limiting, the nutrient sensing pathways are inactivated and their inhibitory influence on autophagy is released.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about nutrient sensing pathways.
